text: When Dale knocked with the surveyor's map rolled under his arm, I already knew what he would find. He spread it on my porch table, weighed the corners with my coffee mug and a flowerpot, and traced the line with a thick finger, frowning. "Funny," he said. "The old stake should be about three feet further your way." I made a sound that was supposed to be surprise. Six summers ago, digging out the hydrangeas, I had pulled that stake, tossed it in the wheelbarrow, and planted it again where it suited my garden. Dale had just lost his wife then. He never noticed. Now he was talking about cedar panels, about splitting the cost, about how he wanted things done right for once, and I kept nodding while heat crawled up the back of my neck. My hands would not stay still; I refolded a napkin four times. "You okay?" he asked. I told him it was the sun. When he left, I stood at the hydrangeas for a long while, looking at the blooms I had stolen three feet of ground for, and they looked smaller than I remembered.

Harold Brandt watched from behind the kitchen blinds as the Nguyens measured the lot line with a yellow tape. Mrs. Nguyen held one end by the lilac; her husband walked it back toward the street, calling out numbers. Harold knew exactly why they wanted the fence. In April a baseball had gone through their back window, and when Mr. Nguyen had come over asking, Harold had stood in this same doorway and said his grandson had been at camp all week. The boy had been in the yard, glove on, pale as milk. Harold had sent him upstairs and paid nothing. Now the tape snapped back into its case, and Mrs. Nguyen glanced toward his house, and Harold stepped away from the window so fast he knocked a cup off the counter. He swept the shards up on his knees, slowly, his chest tight. When the doorbell rang an hour later, he let it ring twice before answering. Mr. Nguyen only wanted a signature for the permit. Harold signed without reading and kept his eyes on the clipboard. "Six feet should be enough," Mr. Nguyen said kindly. Harold could not bring himself to answer.

The contractor found the crack while digging the first post hole, and I heard him whistle from my side of the yard. "Foundation's split here, ma'am," he called to Priscilla, my neighbor, who came out in her house slippers. "Roots, looks like. Big tree's been pushing on it for years." The big tree was my silver maple. Two years ago an arborist had told me to take it down or at least cut the roots back, and he had specifically mentioned her basement wall. I had gotten a quote, winced at it, and put the paper in a drawer. Priscilla stood there with her hand on her mouth. She is seventy-eight and lives on a pension, and she had only wanted a fence so her grandkids' puppy would stop running into the street. I came over to look, and when she turned to me with that worried face and said, "I don't suppose your tree could have done this," my mouth went completely dry. I heard myself say I'd pay for an inspection. I couldn't make myself say the rest, about the drawer, about the quote. That night I took the paper out and read it over and over.

Amara Okafor kept her sunglasses on while Mr. Lindqvist explained his plans for the fence, though the sky was overcast. He was sorry, he said, to put up something so tall, but the homeowners' association had been sending him letters. Someone had reported his compost heap, then his trailer, then the grass. Three complaints in two months. He had decided a fence would keep him out of trouble. "Whoever it is," he said, rubbing his gray stubble, "I guess they just don't like looking at my yard. Fair enough." Amara's stomach turned over. She had filed every one of those complaints, late at night, irritated by the smell of the compost on a hot evening, typing quickly before she could reconsider. She had imagined a careless man, not this one, who apologized to her for being an eyesore and offered to plant climbing roses on her side so she would have something nice to look at. "You don't have to do that," she said, and her voice came out too high. He insisted. She went inside and sat on the edge of the bathtub with her face in her hands until her tea went cold on the counter.

Mrs. Halvorsen left a note in my mailbox, written in her careful schoolteacher cursive: she was thinking of putting up a fence along our shared line and wanted my opinion before calling anyone. At the bottom, as an afterthought, she wrote, "No need to contribute this time, dear, I know things are tight." This time. Eleven years ago we split the cost of the old picket fence, or rather she paid for it and I promised my half by the end of the summer. Then my son was born, then the car died, then I simply stopped bringing it up, and she never did either. I stood at the mailbox reading that line again and again, the paper getting soft from my thumbs. I could see her through her kitchen window, bent over a crossword. I went inside and opened my banking app and stared at the balance, doing math that did not need doing. Then I wrote a check, tore it up because the amount looked stingy, and wrote another. My hand shook a little as I signed it. Walking over, I rehearsed apologies under my breath and none of them sounded good enough.

Every morning that week, Teodoro Ruiz heard the post-hole digger next door, the slow crunch of it, then a grunt, then a pause long enough to worry about. Bill was seventy-four, two years older than Teodoro, with a bad hip, and back in March over beers Teodoro had clapped him on the shoulder and said, "When you do that fence, I'm your man." Then his daughter had visited, and then his back had started acting up, or so he had told himself, and now he found reasons to stay inside: the crossword, the radio, a drawer that needed sorting. He sat at the kitchen table with his coffee getting cold and flinched at every thud. Through the window he could see Bill carrying a post by himself, setting it down every few steps. Teodoro's face grew hot. He put on his boots, took them off, and put them on again. By the time he stepped out, Bill was sitting on a stack of boards, mopping his forehead. "Morning," Bill said, without any edge at all, and somehow that was worse. Teodoro picked up the far end of the next post without a word and could not look at him.

The envelope from Mr. Castellano was thicker than usual, and I opened it standing at the counter with my coat still on. Lease renewal, it said, and then, in a separate paragraph, that due to repeated noise complaints from the unit below, he would not be offering the reduced rate he had mentioned. I read it twice. The unit below was Mrs. Feld, who works nights at the hospital and sleeps in the afternoons. I knew she slept in the afternoons. She had told me so, gently, on the stairs, back in the spring, and I had said of course, and then I had kept practicing drums every day at three because that was when I got home. Twice she had slid notes under my door, and I had stuck them to the fridge and kept playing. They were still there, under a pizza magnet. I took them down now and smoothed them flat. Her handwriting was small and apologetic: "So sorry to bother you again." My face burned. I sat on the floor next to the drum kit with the lease in my lap and could not stop picturing her lying awake with a pillow over her head, counting the beats.

Rafael Mendes read the landlord's letter on the bus, and halfway through, he had to put it down on his knee and look out the window. The building was being sold, the letter said, and the new owner would need the units vacated by spring. All tenants would receive the same notice. He thought immediately of Señora Paz on the fourth floor, eighty-one, who had lived there for thirty years. Two months ago, at a tenants' meeting in her apartment, she had begged everyone to sign a petition against the sale, and Rafael had taken the clipboard, looked at it, and handed it back. He hadn't wanted to make trouble with the landlord, who had promised him a parking spot. He had said he would think about it. He had not thought about it. The petition had fallen two signatures short; he'd heard that at the mailboxes and walked away quickly. Now the bus lurched and his stomach went with it. When he got home, he took the stairs past his own floor, up to the fourth, and stood outside her door with his fist raised for a long time before he knocked, his heart pounding.

I knew the letter was about the carpet before I opened it, and I was right. The landlord, Ms. Whitaker, had done the annual inspection while I was at work, and her note was polite, almost warm: she had noticed the large stain in the bedroom and was so sorry to hear about the leak from upstairs; she would be filing it with the insurance and charging the upstairs tenant for replacement. There had been no leak. There had been a bottle of red wine and a party I wasn't supposed to have, and when she'd asked me in passing last month, I'd said, "Oh, I think something dripped from the ceiling." I had said it so casually. The upstairs tenant is a quiet guy named Ivo who carries his bicycle up three flights every day and always holds the door. I could hear him moving around above me now, footsteps creaking. I put the letter face down on the table. Then I picked it up again. My chest felt like it was full of wet sand. I pulled up Ms. Whitaker's number and my thumb hovered over it, trembling, for a long, long minute.

The letter said only that Mrs. Achterberg had passed away and that her son would now be managing the property, and that rent should be sent to a new address. Liang Wei read it at the mailboxes and then stood there long after the hallway light timed out. Mrs. Achterberg had rented him the apartment four years ago for far less than it was worth because, she said, she liked the look of him. She used to call every few weeks to ask if the heat was working, and lately he'd been letting those calls go to voicemail. The last one was in September. "Just checking in, dear, nothing urgent, call when you can." He had meant to. He had a voicemail he had never played all the way through. Back upstairs, he sat on the edge of the bed and pressed play. Her voice was thinner than he remembered, and she asked whether he might have time to help her change a light bulb in the hallway; she didn't like the ladder anymore. He listened to the message three times, his jaw clenched, staring at the floorboards between his socks.

Gabriela found the landlord's letter on the mat, and her first feeling was relief: rent was staying the same for another year. Then she saw the second page. Mr. Osei had written personally, by hand, thanking her for being such a reliable tenant and for keeping the place so tidy, and asking if she'd be willing to show the downstairs unit to prospective renters since she was so trustworthy. Her cheeks went hot. For the past eight months, while he lived overseas, her boyfriend had been staying with her, unlisted, against the lease, and she'd been subletting the spare room on weekends to strangers off an app. She had told herself it hurt no one. She sat down on the stairs in the hallway and read the word trustworthy again, his slanted letters, the little drawing of a sun he had added by his signature. Upstairs, through the door, she could hear one of the weekend guests rolling a suitcase across the floor. She pressed the letter flat against her knee and kept pressing, as if she could iron something out of it, and did not go up for a long time.

I didn't recognize the return address at first, and then I did: it was the building in Leeds I'd left two years ago, the flat I'd moved out of in the middle of the night. The letter was from Mr. Pryce, the landlord, who was not angry. That was the thing. He wrote that he'd finally tracked me down, that he hoped I was well, that he understood times had been hard. He'd covered the four months of unpaid rent himself, he said, and the cleaning, and the broken cupboard, and he wasn't asking for it back. He only wanted to return a box of my things he'd kept in his garage: some books, my grandmother's teapot, a framed photo. Could I tell him where to send it? I sat at the kitchen table with the letter in front of me, both hands wrapped around a mug I didn't drink from. I remembered him bringing over soup once when I'd had the flu. My throat ached. I got out a pen and paper and started writing back, and crossed out the first line, and the second, and the third, and still had not managed a single honest sentence by midnight.

The board flipped from 6:40 to DELAYED and the whole gate groaned at once, but I just sat there with my phone heavy in my hand. My sister had called twice this morning. I hadn't picked up because I knew what she wanted: for me to come to Dad's birthday dinner last weekend, the one I'd skipped claiming a work conference. There had been no conference. I had stayed home and watched television because I didn't feel like driving four hours and making small talk. Now I was flying out for a real trip, and the only thing I could think about was her voice on the voicemail she left Sunday night: "He kept looking at the door." Around me, people were calling their families, sighing, rebooking. A little girl was asleep across two seats, her father's jacket over her. I scrolled to my sister's number and couldn't press it. I bought a coffee I didn't want just to have something to do with my hands, and burnt my tongue on it, and almost welcomed the sting. Outside, the plane sat at the jet bridge, and the delay kept growing, and every extra minute felt like a minute I'd owed somebody else.

Yusuf Demir had been rude to the gate agent, and he knew it the moment the words left his mouth. "Do you even know how to do your job?" The young woman behind the counter had blinked, said, "I'm very sorry, sir," and typed something with her eyes lowered. Now, forty minutes later, he sat by the window pretending to read, watching her handle the line. A man was yelling at her about his connection; she apologized to him, too. When there was a break, she ducked under the counter and he saw her press the heel of her hand against one eye. Yusuf's newspaper crinkled in his tight grip. He thought of his own daughter, who worked a customer service job in Ankara and called home some nights near tears. He replayed the way he had leaned over the counter, the sneer in his voice. His neck felt hot under his collar. He got up, bought a box of chocolates from the duty-free shop, and stood near the counter holding it, the cellophane slippery under his fingers, waiting for a gap in the line and feeling more foolish with every passing second.

Of all the days for the flight to be delayed, it had to be this one, because now I had three extra hours to think. My brother's wedding was tomorrow afternoon. I'd been asked to give a toast. Last month, after too much wine, I'd told his fiancée something he had told me in confidence, about the panic attacks he'd had in college, and she'd asked him about it, and he had gone very quiet on the phone with me afterwards and said, "I just didn't think you'd do that." He hadn't mentioned it since. He'd still asked me to give the toast. I sat on the floor of the terminal by an outlet, laptop open to a document titled toast_draft_final, and I couldn't write a single line. Every sentence about loyalty or trust or being there for each other made my stomach clench. Somewhere a baby was crying, then stopped. I closed the laptop, opened it, closed it again. I kept picturing him at the front of the room, looking out at me while I stood up, waiting to see what I'd say.

The delay was two hours and then four, and somewhere in the third hour Ingrid realized she had to tell her colleague. Tomas was sitting two seats over at the gate, working on the slides for tomorrow's pitch, the one they had been preparing for months. He had no idea that she'd already been offered a job with the company they were pitching to, or that she had accepted it last Thursday, or that the meeting tomorrow was partly a formality for her. He kept asking her opinion. "Does the color scheme seem too loud?" he said, turning the screen toward her. "You've got a better eye." She said it looked great, and her voice sounded thin. She went to the restroom and stood at the sink running cold water over her wrists, looking at herself in the mirror. When she came back he had bought her a sandwich, her usual, turkey with no tomatoes. He had remembered. She thanked him, took one bite, and it sat in her mouth like paper. She watched the gate board instead of his face, while he kept working, humming quietly.

I told the airline my mother was sick so they'd rebook me first. She isn't sick. She's in Phoenix playing pickleball, probably. But the line was enormous, and the man in front of me was explaining that he was trying to get to a funeral, and somehow when the agent turned to me, I heard myself say, "My mom's in the hospital," and my voice even cracked a little, convincingly. The agent's face softened. She put me on the next flight out, the last seat, and said, "I hope she's okay." Behind me, I heard her tell the funeral man that the flight was now full. He said, "Okay," very quietly, and nothing else. I walked to the new gate without feeling my legs. I kept glancing back, half expecting to see him, half hoping. My boarding pass was damp in my fist. When they called my zone, I let three other zones go ahead of me, standing near the window with my jaw tight, telling myself I could still go back, still give him the seat, and not moving.

Mei Lin got the text about the delay just as she'd settled in at the bar, and her first, ugly reaction was relief. Three more hours before she had to land and face her father's apartment, the hospice nurse, her brother who had been doing everything alone for eight months while she sent money and messages and said work was impossible right now. Work had not been impossible. It had been easier. She ordered a second glass of wine and then pushed it away untouched. Her brother texted: "Delayed? No worries. He's sleeping a lot. I'll tell him you're coming." She stared at the screen until the letters blurred. He didn't sound angry. He never did. He had changed their father's sheets, learned to manage the morphine, slept on a cot. She remembered hearing him on the phone last month, exhausted, asking if she might come for a weekend, and how she had talked about a deadline. Her hands were cold around the glass. She typed "I'm so sorry" and deleted it, then typed it again, and finally sent nothing, just watched the departure board crawl.

The doctor said the word cirrhosis carefully, the way you'd set down something fragile, and I nodded like I'd been expecting it. I hadn't been expecting it for me. I'd been expecting it, years ago, for my wife, who used to beg me to stop. "Please, for the kids," she'd say, standing at the sink while I opened the second bottle. I'd told her she was nagging. I'd told her I was fine. She'd moved out when our youngest was twelve. Now the doctor was talking about transplant lists and lifestyle changes and I was thinking about my daughter's graduation, how I'd shown up with liquor on my breath and she'd looked at me across the gym with her face going stiff. The paper with the test results shook a little in my hands. "Do you have someone who can support you through this?" the doctor asked. I thought of my phone, my contacts, the people I'd let down one at a time. My throat closed. I said yes, my family, and the lie sat heavy in my chest as I walked out into the bright parking lot.

Anjali Rao had been tested because her sister insisted, and now the counselor was telling her she carried the gene. Not just that: it was the same one their mother had. Their mother, who had died at fifty-two, who had asked Anjali to come home that last year, and Anjali, in her second year of residency, had said she could not get away. She had visited exactly once, for two days, and spent most of it on her laptop. Her sister had done the rest: the appointments, the night vomiting, the hospice forms. The counselor was explaining options, screening intervals, preventive surgery, and Anjali, who was a doctor herself, couldn't follow the words. All she could see was her sister's face in the hospital corridor, gray with exhaustion, saying, "It's fine, I know you're busy." Anjali had let her say it. She'd let her say it every time. In the car afterwards, she held the steering wheel without turning the key, her knuckles pale, and then she called her sister, who answered on the first ring, and Anjali found she had nothing to say except, "Can I come over?"

It was negative. The nurse said it twice because I didn't react the first time. "Your results are negative, Mr. Kowalczyk, you're completely clear." I said thank you. I said great. And then I went and sat in my car in the clinic garage and could not make myself start it. Because I'd been tested after the conference in Prague, and the reason I'd been tested was the woman I'd met at the hotel bar, and the reason I'd been so frightened the last two weeks wasn't only the illness. It was the thought of having to tell Joanna. Now I didn't have to tell her anything. That was the clean, simple fact, and I kept turning it over and it felt filthy in my hands. My phone buzzed. Joanna: "How did the checkup go? Making lasagna tonight. Love you." There was a little heart. I stared at it until the screen dimmed. Then I typed "All fine!" and sat there with my thumb hovering, the car cold around me, unable to press send and unable to delete it.

The pediatrician said Leo's lead levels were very high, and Fatima felt the floor go soft under her. "Does your home have old paint? Any renovations recently?" Yes. Yes, her husband had sanded the window frames in the nursery in the spring, and she had said it would be fine, they'd open the windows, Leo would nap downstairs. Except she'd let him crawl into the nursery a dozen times while she folded laundry and answered emails. She remembered the fine white dust on his knees. She had brushed it off with her hand and laughed. Leo was sitting on her lap now, chewing on the corner of a picture book, his warm weight against her stomach. The doctor kept talking, gently, about treatment and testing and that it wasn't anyone's fault, and Fatima kept nodding with her lips pressed together. She held Leo tighter, until he squirmed and protested, and she loosened her grip and kissed the top of his head over and over and whispered sorry into his hair, so quietly the doctor pretended not to hear.

My father opened the envelope from the lab at the kitchen table, put on his reading glasses, and then took them off again. "Well," he said. "Diabetes. Type two." He laughed a little, embarrassed. I didn't laugh. Every Sunday for three years I've brought him a box of pastries from the bakery on Carver Street, the ones with the custard he loves. It started as a way to make up for not visiting during the week. Then it became the whole visit: I'd drop off the box, sit for twenty minutes, and leave feeling generous. His doctor had warned him about his blood sugar last year. He'd told me. I'd said, "One box a week won't hurt." I looked at the pastry box on the counter now, the string still tied, and my face went hot. He followed my eyes. "Don't you dare start blaming yourself," he said, and patted my hand. That made it worse. I picked up the box and held it in my lap like I could hide it, and I asked him how often he'd have to check his levels, and my voice came out small.

Brendan's scan came back clear, and the first thing he felt, before the relief, was a lurch in his gut. He'd been dodging this appointment for two years, and all that time his brother Callum had been nagging him, sending articles, booking appointments for him that Brendan cancelled. Their dad had died of colon cancer at fifty-five. Callum had been the one who'd gotten himself screened at forty and found something early. Brendan had told him he was paranoid, a hypochondriac, had made jokes about it at Christmas in front of everyone, and Callum had gone quiet and set down his fork. Then Callum got sicker this autumn, the thing had come back, and he had stopped nagging, because he didn't have the energy anymore. That was why Brendan had finally come in. He looked at the clean report and could hardly bear it. He drove straight to Callum's house without calling first, and when his brother opened the door, thin, in a robe, Brendan held out the paper like an offering, and his eyes stung, and he couldn't get a single word out.

The A was circled in red at the top of the page, and Mr. Delgado had written "Outstanding work, Noor!" underneath, with an exclamation point. I folded the paper in half before anybody could see. Last Thursday, I'd found the answer key on the printer in the library, still warm, and I'd taken a picture of it with my phone, telling myself I'd just glance. I hadn't just glanced. Now Mr. Delgado was walking down the rows, handing back tests, and when he passed Danny, who studies every lunch and still got a C, he put a hand on his shoulder and said, "Come see me after, we'll figure it out." Danny's ears went pink. My stomach felt like it had dropped through the chair. The fluorescent lights were buzzing. I kept my eyes on the folded paper, running my thumbnail along the crease until it was razor sharp. When class ended, Mr. Delgado smiled at me on the way out and said he'd recommend me for the advanced section next year, and I said thank you without looking up, and my voice cracked on the second word.

Kofi got his chemistry exam back with a 94 and couldn't enjoy it for even a second, because Jaylen, next to him, had gotten a 51 and was staring at it like he'd been slapped. They had studied together the night before. Or rather, Jaylen had come over to study, and Kofi, tired and wanting him gone, had explained the stoichiometry section wrong on purpose, quickly, sloppily, just to make the evening end. He hadn't really thought it through. He'd thought Jaylen would check the book. Jaylen hadn't. Now Jaylen leaned over and said quietly, "Bro, I did it exactly how you showed me," without any accusation, just confusion, and Kofi felt heat crawl up his throat. He looked at question seven, worth twenty points, the one he'd gotten right and Jaylen had gotten wrong, using the method Kofi had invented on the spot. He shoved his test into his backpack. "I must've mixed it up," he said, and his voice was strange. All through the rest of class he tapped his pencil against his knee, staring at the clock, rehearsing a confession he didn't know how to begin.

Professor Hartley handed back the midterms and said, before she passed out a single one, "I want to say something about honesty." My hands went cold. Then she held up a test and said that one student had come to her office and pointed out that she'd marked a wrong answer correct, and given back the points. "That's integrity," she said, and the class clapped for whoever it was, and I clapped too. My exam had the same error. I'd noticed it two weeks ago when we went over the answers, and I'd kept quiet, because those six points were the difference between a B-plus and an A-minus, and my scholarship needs a 3.5. I sat there with my hands still raised from clapping, then lowered them slowly into my lap. The girl next to me was smiling. Professor Hartley was walking up and down the aisles now, and when she set my paper down in front of me, the red check mark next to question four looked enormous, like a stain. I put my hand flat over it and left it there for the rest of the hour.

Ms. Pereira returned the essays and stopped at Wren's desk. "This one," she said, not quietly, "is the best thing anyone's written for me in years." Wren mumbled a thank you and turned the paper over, and the back of her neck prickled. She had written it, technically. But the central idea, the whole argument about the lighthouse as a kind of mother, had come from her older brother's college essay, which she'd found on the family computer. She hadn't copied a sentence. She had just taken the thought, the best part, the part Ms. Pereira had written "brilliant!!" beside in the margin. Now her teacher was asking if she could read it aloud at the district showcase next month. The class turned to look. Wren felt her face go blotchy and red. "I don't know," she said. "I'm not very good at reading out loud." Ms. Pereira laughed warmly and said she'd help her practice. After class, Wren stayed in her seat, picking at a loose thread on her sleeve until it unraveled, the essay a hot weight in her backpack.

I failed the calculus final, which I'd expected, and then I opened the envelope from the school with my semester grades, which my parents had already seen. Mom was at the table with it. She'd taken a second shift at the laundromat all spring to pay for the tutor. Every Tuesday and Thursday, she'd dropped me off at the library, and every Tuesday and Thursday, after she'd driven away, I had walked across the street to Marco's house to play video games, and the tutor, who was a college kid and didn't care, had signed the attendance sheets anyway because I'd asked him to. Mom didn't yell. She looked tired. She said, "Was the tutor not good?" and I said I guessed not, and she nodded and said she'd find a better one, and started going through her purse for the receipts, flattening each one out on the table with her rough, cracked hands. I couldn't stand to watch her do it. I went to my room and lay down on the bed with my shoes on, staring at the ceiling, my chest tight, listening to her count.

Mr. Haddad gave the exams back at the end of the period, and Simone's had a big zero across the top, and a note: "See me. Same answers as another student." Simone felt herself go hot all over. Across the room, Ruby was looking at her own test with her eyes wide, then glancing over. Ruby had a zero too. Simone knew why. She had copied from Ruby's paper, leaning a little to the left during the exam, and Ruby had not known; Ruby was just a fast, careful writer who kept her paper flat on the desk. Now Ruby was raising her hand, her voice shaky, saying, "But I didn't—" and Mr. Haddad said they'd talk after class, both of them. Ruby's chin was trembling. She was the kind of student who cried when she got a B. Simone sat very still, gripping the edges of her desk, her pulse thudding in her ears. When the bell rang, Ruby walked toward the front with her head down, and Simone stood up on legs that didn't feel like her own and followed, every step taking more effort than the last.

I saw Esther before she saw me, by the oranges, and my first instinct was to turn my cart around. We'd been inseparable in our twenties. Then her husband left, and she'd called me night after night, and I had started letting the phone ring, because it was exhausting and I had a new job and a new boyfriend and her sadness felt like a weight I didn't want. I'd stopped calling back entirely. That was nine years ago. Now she looked up, and her face lit, genuinely lit, and she said my name like it was good news. She hugged me right there in produce, smelling of the same vanilla lotion. "I've thought about you so much," she said. I said, "Me too," and the words felt flimsy. She told me she'd gotten through it, remarried, had a little boy. She showed me pictures on her phone. I kept smiling and nodding, my cheeks aching, my hand gripping the cart handle. When she said, "We should get coffee," I said yes too quickly, and walked away to the cereal aisle and stood there staring at boxes without seeing any of them.

Thabo was reaching for the last carton of eggs when someone said, "Thabo Nkosi? No way." It was Pieter, from school, broader now, gray at the temples, grinning like nothing had ever happened. Thabo's grin came a second late. In their final year, someone had stolen money from the class trip fund, and the headmaster had found the envelope in Pieter's locker, and Pieter had been expelled two months before exams. Thabo had put it there. He had taken the money himself, panicking, and stuffed it into the nearest open locker when he heard footsteps. He had told himself for twenty-five years that Pieter would have been fine. Now Pieter was clapping his shoulder, saying he'd ended up driving trucks, couldn't complain, had three kids. "Never did finish school," he said with a shrug. "That whole mess, eh?" Thabo's hand tightened on the egg carton until he felt one crack. "Yeah," he said hoarsely. "That whole mess." Pieter asked if he wanted to grab a beer sometime. Thabo said sure, and wrote his number on Pieter's receipt with a pen that kept skipping because his hand would not stop trembling.

"Is that you, Mags?" Nobody's called me Mags since college, and I turned around holding a jar of pickles and there was Delphine, in scrubs, a basket on her arm. We'd been roommates for three years. At her wedding I was supposed to be the maid of honor, and two weeks before, I backed out, because I'd been offered a trip to Bali with a man I barely knew and I couldn't stand the thought of missing it. I texted her. I didn't even call. She'd written back one line, "Okay," and that was the last I'd heard. Now she was smiling at me, a little cautiously, and asking how I'd been. I talked too fast about my job, my apartment, my cat, as if filling the air would keep anything else from getting in. She mentioned she'd been divorced for two years. "It didn't stick," she said lightly. I felt something tighten in my chest, absurdly, like my absence had been part of it. I put the pickle jar down on a shelf of soup, where it didn't belong, and then I asked her, very quietly, if she'd let me buy her lunch.

Oksana nearly dropped her basket when she saw Mrs. Ilyina by the bread, older now, leaning on the shopping cart for balance. They had been close once, neighbors and friends, until Oksana moved across town and simply never visited. She'd meant to. Then Mrs. Ilyina's husband died, and Oksana heard about it a month later and didn't send a card, because by then it felt too late, and then it felt even later. She had thought about it at strange times, in the shower, at red lights, the card she never wrote. Now the old woman looked up and recognized her slowly, her face folding into a smile. "Oksanochka," she said, and reached out to touch her cheek with a cool, papery hand. Oksana's eyes stung. She started to explain, to apologize, and found she couldn't say her husband's name without her voice wobbling. Mrs. Ilyina just patted her arm. "You were busy," she said. "Young people are busy." Oksana carried her bags out to the car for her and held them far longer than needed, and drove home with the radio off.

I almost didn't recognize Ravi; he'd lost a lot of weight, and he was wearing a uniform from the warehouse across the highway. We'd started a company together at twenty-six, a little app for tracking freight, and when an investor came along who wanted only one founder, I'd let them write Ravi out. I'd told myself it was business. He'd kept a small share, technically. The company sold four years later, and I bought a house with a lake view. Now he was in front of me in the checkout line with a basket of instant noodles and milk, and he turned and saw me, and there was a moment I watched him decide whether to be friendly. He decided to be. "Hey, man," he said. "You look good." I said he did too, which was a lie, and I could feel myself flushing up to my ears. He asked about my family; I gave short answers. The cashier rang him up and his card was declined once, and he laughed it off and tried another. I stood behind him with my full cart, organic everything, and wanted to disappear into the floor.

Hannah Goldberg and her old friend Celeste met in the frozen aisle, both reaching for the same brand of dumplings, and they laughed before they even recognized each other. Then they did, and Hannah's laugh caught in her throat. Five years ago, Celeste had told her a secret about her marriage, something private and painful, and Hannah had repeated it at a book club, framed as a concern, and it had gotten back to Celeste's husband within the week. The friendship had ended with one sharp phone call. Now Celeste was looking at her with an expression Hannah couldn't read, the freezer door fogging between them. "Hi," Celeste said. "Hi," Hannah said, and her voice came out barely above a whisper. She wanted to say a dozen things. She wanted to explain that she'd thought about it every time she opened her mouth at a party since, that she'd left the book club, that she was sorry. What she said was, "These are the good ones," holding up the dumplings, and Celeste nodded, and Hannah stood holding the cold bag so long her fingers went numb.

The engine made a sound like a coin in a blender and then nothing, and I coasted onto the shoulder with the hazards ticking. I knew exactly what it was. Three weeks ago my son, Mateo, had told me the car was making a weird noise, and that he'd checked online and it might be the timing belt, and could I please take it in. I had laughed at him. I'd said he watched too many videos. He is sixteen and wants to be a mechanic, and he'd gone quiet and gone to his room, and I hadn't thought about it again. Now I sat there with trucks shaking the car as they passed, and I called work, and then I called the tow company, and then I sat with my phone in my hand thinking about calling Mateo. I imagined telling him he was right. I imagined how he'd try not to look pleased, how he'd say it's fine, Dad. My eyes stung. When I finally dialed and he answered, sleepy, I said, "Hey, buddy, I need your advice," and he went quiet for a moment, and my chest ached in the silence.

Cormac's car died at the light on Fifth Street, and while he sat there pumping the gas pedal uselessly, he noticed the fuel needle resting below empty. His wife had borrowed the car last night and asked him that morning, "Did you fill it up? You said you would." He'd said yes without looking up from his phone. Now he was blocking traffic, horns blaring, and the woman in the car behind him got out and offered to help push. She was in a suit, older, and she leaned her shoulder against his bumper without hesitation. Cormac steered and she pushed until they reached a parking lot, and she was breathing hard and smiling, and said, "Happens to all of us." He thanked her too many times. Then he called his wife to come with a gas can, and when she asked what happened, he said, "No idea, it just stalled," and immediately felt his face heat up. She said she'd be right there and that she loved him. He sat on the curb in the bright morning, elbows on his knees, staring at a crack in the asphalt.

I was the one who told Shirin her car was fine. She'd bought it from me, my old hatchback, two months ago, and when she asked about the transmission, I'd said, "Never had a problem," which wasn't true; it had been slipping since the winter. I needed the money for the deposit on my apartment. This morning she called me from the side of the highway, close to tears, because it had died on the way to her new job, her first day, and she didn't know who else to call. I drove out there. She was sitting on the guardrail in her nice blazer, mascara smudged, and when she saw me she stood up and hugged me, grateful, and said, "I'm so sorry to bother you." I couldn't look at her. I popped the hood and pretended to examine things I already understood perfectly. My hands were sweaty on the metal. I drove her to her office and she ran in, forty minutes late. Then I sat in the parking lot with the engine running, my stomach churning, doing the math on what a new transmission would cost me to pay for.

Deshawn's car broke down two miles from the office, and he was relieved. He knew how that sounded. He sat on the hood waiting for the tow truck and let the relief wash over him, followed immediately by something sour. Today was the day he was supposed to present the quarterly numbers, numbers he'd fudged, just slightly, to cover a mistake he'd made in June. His colleague Priya had noticed something off last week and asked him about it, and he'd brushed her off, said she must be reading the wrong spreadsheet, and she'd apologized to him. Now, stuck here, she would have to present in his place. She'd stand up there with his slides. If anyone noticed, she'd be the one answering questions. He pictured her at the front of the conference room, trying to explain figures that didn't make sense, her face going red. He picked up his phone, scrolled to her number, and put it down. Picked it up again. A semi rushed past and rocked the car. Finally he called her, and when she answered, cheerful, he swallowed hard and asked if she had a minute.

My car stalled in the middle of a rainstorm, and I sat there with the wipers dead, watching the water sheet down the glass, and the only person I could think of to call was my father. We hadn't spoken in fourteen months. The last time, he'd asked to borrow money for his rent, and I'd said no, harshly, said he'd never paid anything back in his life, which wasn't true. He'd paid for my first car. This car, in fact; he'd helped me pick it out. I called him anyway. He answered on the second ring and said, "What's wrong?" because I would only call if something was wrong, and he knew it. Twenty minutes later his old truck pulled up, and he got out in the rain without a coat, sixty-eight years old, and leaned under my hood with a flashlight in his teeth. He fixed something with a wrench and a piece of wire. "Should get you there," he said. I sat dripping in the driver's seat, my throat thick, and asked how the rent situation had turned out, and he said, "Oh, it worked out," and didn't look at me.

When the car shuddered and died on the overpass, Aiko Tanaka's first thought was the bus driver. Last month, late and furious, she'd filed a complaint against the driver on her usual route, claiming he'd been rude, when actually he'd only told her, reasonably, that she couldn't board through the back door. She'd heard from another regular that he'd been suspended for a week without pay. He had a little photo of his daughters taped by the fare box. Now her car was dead and she'd have to take that bus to work for the next several days while it was repaired. She stood at the stop in the drizzle, umbrella dripping, her shoulders tight, praying it would be a different driver. It wasn't. He looked at her as she climbed up, and she couldn't tell if he recognized her. "Morning," he said evenly. She tapped her card and slid into a seat near the back, and the whole ride she stared at the back of his head, the gray hairs at his collar, and kept rubbing her thumb over the clasp of her bag until it hurt.

It's after one, and Zara isn't home, and I keep checking my phone even though I've turned the volume all the way up. The last thing I said to her, at dinner, was that she was selfish and that I was tired of her treating this house like a hotel. I said it in front of her little brother. I slammed my fork down. She left without a word, and I let her, because I was too angry to stop her. Now the anger is gone and there's just the clock on the stove, 1:14, and the sound of the refrigerator humming. I keep replaying her face, the way it closed off. She's seventeen. She was trying to tell me something about her friend's mother being sick, and I didn't let her finish, because I'd already decided what kind of night it was going to be. I've texted her four times. The first one says "Where are you?" The last one says "I'm sorry, please just let me know you're okay." It still shows unread. I'm sitting on the stairs in my bathrobe, my knees pulled up, staring at the front door.

Gerald sat in the dark living room with the television on mute, the remote in his hand, watching the headlights of every car that turned onto their street. His son Emeka had borrowed the car for a party, and Gerald had said yes too quickly, mostly because he wanted to watch the game without being interrupted. He hadn't asked who would be there. He hadn't asked if there'd be drinking. He hadn't reminded him to text. Emeka's mother would have asked all of those questions, and she was on a work trip in Lagos, and she had told Gerald before she left, "Please be strict with him, he's testing everything." He'd laughed and said he could handle one weekend. Now it was a quarter to two. Gerald got up, walked to the window, and walked back, and his knees cracked. He dialed Emeka again and got voicemail. He considered calling his wife and imagined her voice, the long pause, and put the phone face down on the coffee table. When at last the headlights swept the wall and the engine cut off, his whole body sagged, and he turned his face from the boy so he wouldn't see how badly his hands were shaking.

I check her location on my phone, the way I have every night for six months, and then I put the phone down and stare at the clock. She doesn't know I can see where she is. When I set up her phone, I turned the sharing on and hid the icon, and I've told myself it's for her safety, but it's also because I read her messages one night last year and found out she was seeing a boy she'd told me was just a friend. I never told her I'd read them. I just started tracking her. Tonight the dot sits at the library, which is where she said she'd be, studying for her exams. The library closes at eleven; it's 11:40. She's probably walking home. She hasn't lied to me once, in all these months of watching. I've checked every night and she has been exactly where she said she would be, every single time. My stomach is in knots. When I hear her key in the lock, I quickly close the app, shove the phone under a cushion, and pick up a book I'm not reading, and my cheeks are burning when she comes in and kisses my forehead.

Rosalind waited in the kitchen with a cup of chamomile tea that had gone cold an hour ago. Her daughter Poppy was out past curfew, and Rosalind knew where she was: at her father's apartment across town. Poppy went there sometimes after school, and Rosalind had spent years making it hard. Canceling weekends at the last minute. Telling Poppy her dad was unreliable. Saying things, small, poisonous things, in the car. Tonight Poppy had texted at nine, "At Dad's, he's teaching me to drive, back by 11," and Rosalind had written back a long, furious message about rules, and Poppy had replied, "Why do you always do this?" and then gone silent. Now it was half past midnight. Rosalind turned her mug in slow circles on the counter. She remembered Poppy at six, crying at the window waiting for her dad's car, and herself saying, "See? He's not coming," when in fact she'd told him the wrong time. Her throat burned. At last she picked up her phone, scrolled to her ex-husband's number, which she hadn't dialed in years, and pressed it, and listened to it ring, her heart pounding.

It's three in the morning and my son is still out, and the thing I can't stop thinking about is that I taught him this. Not on purpose. But Dominic is fifteen, and every Friday when he was small, I'd go out after work and come home late and loud, and his mother would be waiting at this same table, in this same chair, with this same look on her face, and I'd laugh and say, "Relax, I'm home, aren't I?" I sat in the car on the driveway some nights just so I wouldn't have to face her. Now I'm the one in the chair. I've called his phone eleven times. Every time a car passes, my heart lurches into my throat. I keep thinking of his mother, now my ex-wife, and how many nights she sat here exactly like this, and how I never once said sorry, not properly. I pick up my phone and write her a message, the first in two years. I write that I finally understand what I put her through. I sit there with my thumb over the send button, my eyes wet, listening for the door.

Kenji paced the hallway in his socks while the clock in the living room ticked past midnight. His daughter Sakura had gone to a concert, and earlier, when she'd asked him for a ride home, he'd said no. He'd told her she was old enough to figure it out, that he had an early morning. The truth was he hadn't wanted to drive an hour into the city on a Friday night, and he'd been short with her on the phone, irritated by her pleading. She'd said, "Fine," and hung up. Now she wasn't answering, and the news said a train line had been suspended because of an accident downtown. He'd turned the radio off after hearing that. He picked up his car keys from the bowl by the door, then put them down, then picked them up again. The metal was warm from his hand. He thought of her standing on some cold platform in the dark, her phone dying, too proud to call back after how he had spoken. His stomach twisted. He grabbed his coat and went out to the car, and his fingers fumbled twice with the key before it caught.

When Brenda leaned into my cubicle and said, "Do you have a minute? My office," my stomach dropped straight to my shoes. I knew what it was about. Last Thursday, Fiona from accounting had been fired for leaking client information, and everyone was talking about it, saying how awful it was, she had kids, she'd seemed so nice. Fiona hadn't leaked anything. I had forwarded the file to my personal email, careless, to work on it from home, and my email account had been hacked. I'd figured that out on Saturday, sitting at my kitchen table, my coffee going cold. I had not told anyone. I followed Brenda down the hall feeling like my legs were made of wet paper. Inside her office she smiled and said she wanted to offer me Fiona's accounts, since I'd been doing such good work. She slid a folder across the desk. I stared at it. My mouth was dry, and I could hear the clock on her wall ticking, loud. "Is something wrong?" she asked. I put both hands flat on the folder, and I took a long breath, and I started to explain.

Lucía sat across from her manager, Mr. Abernathy, with her hands folded so tightly in her lap that her rings dug into her fingers. He was praising her. The client presentation had gone wonderfully; the regional director had called personally to say the analysis was the best he'd seen all year. "This is the kind of thinking we need on the leadership track," Mr. Abernathy said, beaming. Lucía smiled and felt sick. The analysis was Danielle's. Danielle, the new hire, quiet, who had stayed until ten every night that week, who had emailed Lucía the draft with a timid note asking if it was any good. Lucía had cleaned it up, put it in the company template, and presented it with her own name on the title slide. She'd told herself she'd mention Danielle at the meeting. She hadn't. Now Mr. Abernathy was talking about a promotion, a raise, and through the glass wall of his office, Lucía could see Danielle at her desk, hunched over a keyboard, a sandwich in one hand. Lucía's face felt stiff from smiling. "Actually," she said, and her voice cracked, "there's something I should tell you."

The manager's office smelled like burnt coffee, and I sat in the chair across from Mr. Oyelaran's desk with my heart going like a hammer. He'd called me in to ask about the missing inventory. "Twelve laptops," he said. "Someone signed for them on Tuesday." He turned his monitor toward me. The signature was mine. I hadn't stolen them. But on Tuesday, Kevin, from the loading dock, had asked me to sign for a delivery while he stepped out, and I'd done it without counting, without checking a single box, because I was in a hurry to get to lunch. Kevin had been with the company for twenty years. He'd taught me how to use the scanner. Mr. Oyelaran was watching me. "You signed without checking," he said, not a question. I nodded, and my neck felt hot. "Who was on the dock?" he asked. I opened my mouth and closed it. I thought about Kevin's daughter's wedding photos on his phone. I thought about what I had done, and what I hadn't done, and my hands gripped the arms of the chair until my knuckles went white.

Viktor knew why he was being called in. The email had said only, "Please stop by at 3," but he'd seen HR's Monique walking into the manager's office twenty minutes earlier, carrying a file. Last week he'd written an anonymous review about Svetlana on the internal feedback system. He'd said she was difficult, unprofessional, that she took credit for others' work. It had been petty. He'd been angry because she'd gotten the project lead he wanted. And it had been anonymous, or so he'd thought. At 2:58 he walked down the hall, his shoes squeaking on the floor, his palms clammy. Through the window of the office he could see Svetlana already there, sitting with her back very straight. Her eyes were red. Viktor's chest tightened so sharply he had to stop and put a hand on the wall. Then he realized: she wasn't the one under review. She was the one who'd been called in about the complaint. He'd assumed they'd caught him. They hadn't. Instead she was answering for his words. He stood outside the door, frozen, his hand on the handle, unable to turn it.

My manager, Gloria, closed the door behind me and sat down on the edge of her desk instead of behind it, which is what she does when she's about to be kind. "I know about your mom," she said. "I just wanted to say take whatever time you need." My mom is fine. My mom is perfectly healthy and living in Tucson. Three weeks ago I'd told Gloria she'd had a stroke, because I needed a week off for a job interview in Denver and had run out of personal days. Gloria had sent flowers to my apartment. The whole team signed the card. Now she was telling me she'd been through the same thing with her own father, and that if I needed to talk, her door was always open, and her eyes were shiny. I sat there nodding, picking at the hem of my sweater, my face so hot I was sure she could see it. When she reached over and squeezed my hand, I nearly pulled away. I said, "Thank you, really," and my voice came out wrong, strangled, and Gloria took that for grief.

When the manager called Nasser in, he was already holding his breath. Mrs. Kirkland didn't waste time. "Someone has been clocking in for Jorge on the weekends," she said. "Security footage shows it's your badge." Nasser had done it twice, maybe three times. Jorge had asked him, laughing, said his kid had a game, said nobody would notice. It had felt like a favor between friends. Now Mrs. Kirkland was saying that Jorge had already been let go this morning, that he'd told her it was all his own idea, that Nasser hadn't known what it was for. Nasser hadn't known? Nasser had known exactly. Jorge had protected him. He stared at the carpet, his heart thudding painfully. He thought of Jorge, cleaning out his locker this morning, how Nasser had seen him in the parking lot and Jorge had just raised a hand and waved. "So I'm going to give you a warning," Mrs. Kirkland was saying, "and we'll leave it there." Nasser's mouth opened. He felt sick, his face burning. "No," he said finally, quietly. "That's not how it happened."

The letter was in a shoebox under my old high school yearbooks, addressed to me in my grandfather's shaky handwriting, the envelope already torn open. I remembered now: it had come the spring I was nineteen, the spring I was too busy to visit him in the nursing home. I'd read it once, quickly, standing in my dorm's hallway, and stuffed it in a drawer. Now I sat on the attic floor in the dust and read it properly. He wrote about the garden he'd had to leave. He wrote that he was sorry to be a nuisance but he'd love to see me before the summer, if I could manage, and that he'd saved some of my grandmother's recipes for me. He died in July. I didn't go to see him. I went to the funeral and cried, and everyone said how close we'd been. My hands were trembling around the thin paper. The attic was stifling, and sweat ran down my back, but I couldn't make myself get up. I read it again, and again, the last line especially, which said, "Don't worry if you can't."

Marguerite found the letter tucked inside an old cookbook, and she knew the handwriting before she unfolded it: her sister Odile, whom she hadn't spoken to in nineteen years. The date was 2006. The letter was short. Odile wrote that she was getting help for her drinking, that she was in a program, that she knew she had hurt Marguerite badly but wanted to try. "I'll understand if you can't answer," she wrote. "But I hope you will." Marguerite didn't remember receiving it. Then, slowly, she did. She remembered seeing the return address, feeling her jaw clench, and putting it into the cookbook, unopened, to deal with later. She had never dealt with it. Two years after that, Odile had died in a car accident, and Marguerite had told everyone she'd never tried to reach out. She sat back against a cardboard box, dust motes floating in the slanted light from the attic window, and pressed the letter against her chest. She could hear her own breathing, ragged. Downstairs, her husband called up to ask if she wanted coffee. She couldn't answer. She just kept holding the paper, rocking slightly.

The envelope was from Michelle, my college roommate, and inside was a letter asking me, politely, nervously, to pay back the eight hundred dollars she'd lent me junior year. "I wouldn't ask, but my mom's surgery," she wrote. "Even part of it would help." I remember reading it. I remember being broke and embarrassed and deciding to answer it later, when I had the money. I'd had the money within a year. I had never answered. It was dated 2011. Sitting on the attic floor surrounded by cardboard boxes, I looked her up on my phone, my fingers clumsy. She was a nurse now, in Ohio. There was a photo of her at what looked like a memorial, holding a framed picture of an older woman, and the caption said "Miss you every day, Mama." I put the phone face down on the plywood. My chest felt crushed. The attic was too hot and smelled of mothballs. I thought about how many times she must have checked her mailbox. Then I picked the phone back up and started searching for her address, and my thumbs kept hitting the wrong letters.

Arjun was clearing out his parents' attic before the house sale when he found his own handwriting on an envelope addressed to Mom and Dad. Inside was a letter he'd written at twenty-two, the year he'd left for America without telling anyone until the day before his flight. He'd written it in the airport and posted it from London. He remembered it as an apology. Reading it now, he saw that it wasn't. It was cold, self-righteous, full of accusations: that they had smothered him, that his father's expectations were a cage, that he needed to get away from them. His father had underlined a single sentence in pencil, faintly: "I don't know when I'll come back." Arjun sat down heavily on a trunk. His father had died last March. Arjun had flown in for the funeral and flown out four days later. Now, holding the brittle paper, he imagined his father reading it at the kitchen table, putting on his glasses, taking the pencil from behind his ear. Arjun's eyes burned. He folded the letter very carefully along its old creases, as if neatness could fix anything, and could not stand up for a long while.

I wasn't looking for anything in the attic except the Christmas lights, and then I found the stack of letters from Joanie, rubber-banded together, maybe twenty of them, all from the year after she moved to the coast. My best friend from fourth grade. I flipped through them. The early ones were long, funny, full of drawings. Then they got shorter. The last one, near the bottom, just said, "Did I do something wrong? You can tell me." I had never written back. Not once, not to any of them. I'd been eleven and lazy and had a new best friend and thought she'd just stop eventually, and she had. I sat there under the bare light bulb with the Christmas lights tangled in my lap. Thirty years later, my face was hot, my throat thick, as though I was that same little girl getting caught. I kept thinking of her at the mailbox, checking. I took out my phone and searched her name, and her married name, and every combination I could think of, and when I finally found a profile with her smile, I sat looking at it for twenty minutes before I could type anything.

Emmanuel lifted the lid of the trunk and found the letter on top, as if someone had placed it there for him to find. It was from his first wife, Grace, written thirty years ago, the week after he'd moved out. He had only skimmed it at the time, angry, convinced she was trying to manipulate him. That word came to him now with a wince. He read it slowly in the gray attic light. She didn't accuse him. She wrote that she was pregnant, that she had only found out after he left, that she didn't want anything from him but thought he deserved to know. Emmanuel's hands went cold. He had read it. He must have. He remembered tearing open the envelope at his brother's apartment, scanning the first lines about missing him, and tossing it into a box. He had never read to the end. He had a son, or a daughter, somewhere, nearly thirty years old, who had grown up believing their father simply didn't care. The attic floor creaked under him as he sank down. He sat there, the page shaking in his fingers, breathing in short, sharp gasps.

The roast was in the oven and the doorbell would ring in twenty minutes, and I kept glancing at the seating cards on the table. Eight cards. Not nine. I hadn't invited Lorraine. We've been in the same book group for six years, and all the others were coming tonight, and I'd left her out because she talks too much and laughs too loud, and I wanted one evening without her. I'd told everyone to keep it quiet. This afternoon she'd texted me a photo of a pie she'd baked, asking if I wanted it for anything, since she'd made two. I'd written back, "Aw, so sweet, no plans this weekend though!" and added a smiley face. Now I was basting the meat, and my hand slipped and I burned my wrist on the oven rack, and I held it under the cold tap far longer than I needed to, staring at the steam rising from the sink. Her pie was probably sitting on her kitchen counter. I pictured her eating a slice alone in front of the television. When the doorbell rang, I jumped, and I had to wipe my eyes with a dish towel before I opened the door.

Ibrahim stirred the lentils and checked the clock again. His brother-in-law would be here at seven with the family, and Ibrahim had told his wife he'd made everything from scratch, the way her mother used to. He had not. Half the dishes had come from the Lebanese place on Elm Street, emptied into their good serving bowls, the plastic containers stuffed deep into the outside bin under a bag of grass clippings. It had started as a small thing; work had run late, he'd been tired. But his wife had been so happy this morning, so touched, telling her sister on the phone, "He's been cooking for two days." She had kissed his cheek. Now he stood at the stove, wooden spoon in hand, the kitchen smelling of cumin and garlic, and each time she walked in and said, "It smells like home," he felt his ears go hot. He turned the lentils that didn't need turning. When she asked him to teach her the stuffed grape leaves recipe someday, he coughed, said "Of course," and dropped the spoon on the floor, and bent to get it so she couldn't see his face.

Six guests, seven-thirty, and I was still chopping onions when my phone lit up with a text from my mother: "Have a lovely dinner, darling. I'll be fine on my own, don't worry." Today is the anniversary of my father's death. Three years. I knew that. I'd known it when I planned this dinner party for my new colleagues, and I'd told myself she wouldn't mind, that she'd want me to have a life. I had not called her this morning. I hadn't called yesterday either. I put the knife down. My eyes were streaming, and it wasn't only the onions. I wiped my hands on my apron and looked around the kitchen: the candles, the good wine breathing on the counter, the place cards I'd lettered by hand. My mother was forty minutes away, in the house where we'd lived, probably sitting in his armchair. I picked up the phone and called her. When she answered, her voice was bright, too bright, and she said, "Oh, you didn't have to call, you're busy." I leaned against the fridge and couldn't speak for a moment, and the pot on the stove started to boil over.

Beatriz arranged the cheese board with trembling fingers. Her guests tonight were her husband's parents, and the last time they'd come for dinner, eight months ago, she had served them chicken and, when her mother-in-law asked if it contained nuts because of her allergy, Beatriz had said no without checking the sauce. It had. They'd spent the night in the emergency room. Her mother-in-law had been gracious about it, too gracious, insisting that anyone could have made that mistake. Beatriz couldn't stop thinking about the sound of her wheezing in the car. Tonight she'd read every label in the pantry twice. She'd bought a new cutting board and new knives, and she'd scrubbed the counters with bleach until her hands were raw and red. She'd even called the bakery to ask about their kitchen. Her husband came in, saw her rereading a cracker box, and gently took it from her. "Bea, it's fine," he said. "Mom isn't upset." She nodded, but she picked the box back up the moment he left and read the ingredients again, her lips moving silently, her stomach in a knot.

The lamb has been in the oven for three hours, and the house smells wonderful, and I can't enjoy any of it because the guests tonight are Owen and his new wife. Owen was my closest friend for fifteen years. His last business failed partly because of me. I'd been his partner, the money person, and I'd seen the trouble months before he did, and instead of telling him, I'd quietly pulled my investment out and let him find out from the bank. He lost the restaurant. He lost his house. He's rebuilt since then; he has a food truck now and is married, and when we ran into each other last month, he hugged me and said, "Water under the bridge, man." He accepted my invitation tonight with a thumbs-up emoji. I keep moving the wine glasses a quarter inch to the left, then back again. My hands are sweaty. I've set out his favorite dish, the one he used to make in his kitchen, and now I'm afraid it'll look like I'm trying too hard, which I am. When the doorbell rings, my stomach clenches, and I stand in the hallway for three full breaths before opening it.

Ngozi wiped the counters again, though they were spotless, and peeked at the roast. The guests were her daughter, Adaeze, and Adaeze's girlfriend, coming for dinner for the first time. Two years ago, when Adaeze told her, Ngozi had said terrible things. That it was a phase, that it was a sin, that she should not bring this into the house. She had said it at this table. Adaeze had stopped calling. Ngozi had spent many nights since then sitting on the edge of her bed with the phone in her lap, rereading old messages, listening to the silence in the house. Last month, she had finally written to her daughter. Tonight was the answer. She had cooked jollof rice, the way Adaeze liked it, with the crispy bits at the bottom. She had laid out the good plates, the ones from her wedding. Her hands would not stay still; she straightened the napkins, smoothed the tablecloth, moved a chair. When the car pulled into the driveway, she pressed her palms against her apron and whispered to herself, practicing the first words, the ones she should have said so long ago.

The new apartment has white walls and a view of a parking garage, and I'm sitting on an unopened box because I haven't assembled a single chair yet. My phone keeps lighting up with messages from Thea. We were roommates for four years back home, and three weeks ago I told her I was leaving, two days before I left, even though I'd known for months. She'd had to find a new roommate in a hurry, and the rent went up, and her messages now are kind, which is the worst part. "Hope the move went okay! Send pictures!" I haven't answered. I keep thinking of her face when I told her, standing in our old kitchen, holding a mug I'd given her, and how she said, "Oh," and then, "I'm happy for you," and how she meant it. I was scared she'd talk me out of it, so I didn't let her have the chance. I open her message and start typing an explanation, and it sounds like an excuse. I delete it. I look at the bare walls. My stomach aches, and outside a car alarm starts wailing and won't stop.

Yohannes carried the last box up four flights of stairs into his new apartment in Toronto and set it down, out of breath, in the middle of the empty living room. His phone buzzed. It was his mother, in Addis Ababa, sending a voice message he knew would be full of blessings. She had cried at the airport. His younger sister had cried too, and asked who would help with their father now that his legs were getting weaker. Yohannes had said he'd send money every month. He'd said he'd visit at Christmas. He hadn't mentioned that the plane ticket cost more than a month's rent here, or that he'd taken this job partly because he couldn't stand watching his father struggle on the stairs every morning. He played the message. His mother prayed for his safety, for his health, for his success. Then his father's voice, faint, in the background: "Tell him we're proud." Yohannes sat down on the box. He stared at the bare floorboards, his jaw tight, the phone pressed to his ear long after the message ended, and couldn't make himself call back.

Moving day, and I'm standing in an empty apartment in Chicago that I chose because it is eight hundred miles from my ex-husband and our children's school. I agreed to the custody arrangement. I said I'd fly back twice a month. The kids, Nora and Sam, stood on the porch the day I left, and Sam, who is seven, asked if he could come too, and I said, "Not this time, buddy," and got in the car before my face could crumple. Now I'm unpacking a box of towels and find, wrapped in one of them, a drawing he must have slipped in: a stick figure of me and a stick figure of him, holding hands, under a big yellow sun. My knees give out and I sit down on the bare floor. The new job is a promotion. It's a good job. I keep telling myself that. My hands smooth out the crayon drawing over and over on my thigh. The apartment echoes. I open my laptop and look at flight prices for this weekend, and I start crying when I see they're higher than I expected.

Clémentine had told her grandmother she was moving to Lyon for work. That was only half of it. The other half was that she'd been the one caring for her grandmother for three years, cooking her meals, bringing her to appointments, sleeping in the spare room on bad nights, and she was so tired she'd begun to dream about running away. When the job came up, she took it within an hour. Her aunt was going to move in instead, and was furious about it, and had said so in front of everyone at the farewell lunch. Now Clémentine stood in her new studio with the window open, listening to the noise of the street, the trams, the café below. It should have felt like freedom. Instead she kept picturing her grandmother at the kitchen table, waiting for the soup at noon, the way Clémentine always made it. Her aunt didn't know about the salt; Grand-mère liked it with less. She took out her phone, wrote a long message to her aunt explaining the salt, the pills, the night light, and pressed send, and then sat on the floor, hugging her knees.

I signed the lease, I got the keys, and now I'm sitting on the floor of my new place in Austin eating takeout off the box, and I still haven't told my parents I quit the program. They think I moved here for the residency. I was in my second year of medical school when I left, last spring, and I've let them keep paying the loans every month since. My dad works double shifts at the plant. He tells his friends at church about his son the doctor. He sent me a text this morning: "Proud of you, kiddo. Good luck at the new hospital." With a thumbs-up and a stethoscope emoji he must have searched for. I sat on the edge of the bathtub when I read it, and I couldn't breathe right for a minute. The job I actually have is in software, at a startup, and it pays well, better than residency would have. Still, I can't even bring myself to unpack the box of textbooks I've hauled across three states. It's sitting by the door, the tape unbroken, and I keep looking at it.

Malak had moved to a new city because of what she'd done, and on the first night in the apartment she lay awake on a mattress on the floor, listening to the unfamiliar hum of the refrigerator. Back home, at the clinic, she'd made an error with a medication dose. The patient had recovered, eventually, but the nurse on shift that night, a woman named Hester, had been blamed for it, and Malak had not corrected anyone. She'd let the review board conclude what it concluded. Hester had been transferred to a different ward, a demotion. Malak had resigned two weeks later, citing family reasons, and taken this job across the country. Now she stared at the ceiling, which had a water stain shaped like a bird. Her new colleagues had been friendly at orientation. One had told her she had a trustworthy face. Malak rolled onto her side and pulled the blanket over her head. Her heart was beating too fast. She reached for her phone in the dark and found Hester's email address, which she had saved and never once used, and she began, very slowly, to type.

Mile twenty-five and my legs are full of broken glass, and the only thing keeping me going is the name written on my arm in marker: Gwen. My running partner. We trained together for a year for this race, and three weeks ago she tore her calf on a training run that I insisted on, a hard hill session in the rain when she'd told me she felt a twinge. I told her not to be soft. I'd laughed. She heard the pop. Now she's somewhere in the crowd on crutches, and she made me promise to finish for both of us. I'm wearing the bib with her name on the back. Every time a spectator shouts "Go, Gwen!" because they've read it, my throat closes up. I didn't earn that cheer. The road tilts upward. My lungs burn. I spot her near the barricade, waving one crutch over her head, grinning, shouting my name, and I nearly stop running. I lift a hand, and my face is wet, and I tell myself it's just sweat, and I keep going toward the line she should be crossing.

Kwame's legs were cramping badly with less than a mile to go, and he slowed to a shuffle, his breath ragged. A runner beside him, an older man in a faded club shirt, slowed too and said, "Come on, son, we'll do it together." Kwame recognized him. At mile eighteen, at the water station, Kwame had shoved past this same man to grab a cup, too hard, elbowed him in the ribs, and the man had stumbled and dropped his own water. Kwame had heard him gasp and hadn't looked back. Now the man was jogging next to him, matching his pace, encouraging him. "Breathe out long," the man said. "Lift the knees." Kwame wanted to apologize, but the words stuck in his chest along with the burning. He nodded, kept running, staring at the asphalt. Every kind word was like a pebble in his shoe. With four hundred meters to go, the man said, "You go on ahead, you've got more in you." Kwame turned, panting, and said, "Mile eighteen. That was me," and the man just smiled and waved him forward, and Kwame's eyes blurred as he ran.

The last mile of the marathon passes my old neighborhood, and I didn't know that when I signed up. Turn left on Lambert, past the corner store, and there's the house where my mother still lives. I haven't been inside it in three years. She called on my birthday and I didn't pick up. She called at Christmas and I let it go to voicemail. She didn't do anything terrible, not really; I was just tired of her questions, her worries, her small criticisms. I'm running so slowly now my feet are barely leaving the pavement, and the crowd is thinning, and then there she is, on the porch, in a lawn chair with a homemade sign that says MY DAUGHTER IS RUNNING!!! She must have found out from the race website. She's scanning the runners, squinting. She hasn't spotted me yet. My heart is pounding, not from running. I could put my head down and keep going. I nearly do. Then I veer off the course toward the porch, legs wobbling, and she stands up so fast the chair tips over behind her.

With a mile to go, Siobhan's watch beeped to say she was on pace for a personal best, and she felt a sick twist in her stomach instead of excitement. At mile ten she'd seen a woman go down, collapsed against the curb, face pale, and Siobhan had glanced at her watch and kept running. Someone else would help, she'd thought; there were medics everywhere. She had heard a man shouting for water behind her. She'd gone around a corner and the sound had faded. For sixteen miles she'd been trying not to think about it, and now, so close to the finish, she couldn't think of anything else. Was the woman all right? Had anyone stopped? The crowds were cheering. Somebody rang a cowbell right by her ear. She saw a medical tent off to the right and slowed, then nearly stopped, staring at it. A volunteer called, "You okay? Keep going, you're almost there!" Siobhan nodded and ran on, but her stride had gone loose and heavy, and when she crossed the line, she didn't look up at the clock at all.

I'm going to finish this race, and it'll say three hours forty on the clock, and my name will be on the results page with a time I didn't run. At mile fourteen I cut through the park. Everyone was so packed together, and my knee was screaming, and there was a gap in the barrier, and I saw that the course looped back around the lake, and I just walked through the trees and came out two miles ahead. Nobody saw. Then I came out among runners who'd been far ahead of me, and one of them, a woman with a race shirt that said "Running for Mom—Pancreatic Cancer," cheered me on as I passed her. Now it's the last mile and people are lining both sides, holding out orange slices and gummy bears, and a little boy is holding up a sign that says YOU ARE ALL HEROES. I can't meet his eyes. My chip is going to beep at the finish line like everyone else's. I slow down. I slow down more. Then I stop, right at the edge of the road, and stand there with my hands on my knees, unable to go on.

Tomasz could see the finish banner now, a blurry arch of red and white at the end of the boulevard, and he thought of the training plan his coach had written for him on a napkin last winter. Coach Benedek had been seventy-one and had trained Tomasz for free, out of love for the sport, for nearly two years. Then in September, Tomasz had found a younger, flashier coach online, one with a big following, and he'd sent Benedek a short text saying he wouldn't need him anymore. No call. Benedek had written back, "Good luck, my boy, run with your heart." Two weeks later, he'd had a stroke. He was in a care home now and couldn't speak well. Tomasz hadn't visited. The crowd was roaring and his legs were going numb, and Tomasz kept seeing that napkin, the old man's careful handwriting, the little drawing of a runner. He felt his breath hitch and turn into something like a sob. He crossed the line and didn't stop his watch. He walked straight past the medal table, still gasping, and pulled out his phone to find the address of the care home.
