I left the gate open. I know I did. I was taking the recycling out at seven and I was on the phone with my sister and I propped it with the bin and then I forgot, and now it's nine o'clock and Biscuit hasn't come in, and I've been calling him for twenty minutes. The yard is dark. I've got the flashlight from the junk drawer and I'm sweeping it across the hedges, the shed, the bushes by the fence, and the gate is standing there, wide open, like an accusation. My daughter is upstairs asleep. Biscuit sleeps at the foot of her bed every night. She's going to wake up and ask where he is. I keep calling his name, my voice getting higher and thinner each time, and I shake the treat bag, and nothing. A car goes by on the road, too fast, and my stomach drops through the ground. I walk out the gate and down the street in my slippers, the cold seeping in, calling and calling, and I keep thinking about how I told her I'd be careful.

Paloma stood at the back door, the porch light buzzing above her, calling for Rocco. The old Lab had gone out after dinner and hadn't come back, and for the last hour, she'd been telling herself he was just sniffing around. He was fourteen. He'd been slowing down. The vet had said in October that he needed the heart medication twice a day, and she had been forgetting the evening dose more often than not lately; she'd been working late, eating dinner standing up, falling asleep on the couch. She had told the vet last week, when he asked, that Rocco was getting it every day. Now she walked out into the wet grass, her flashlight shaking, and found him lying by the far fence, on his side under the apple tree, breathing slowly. He thumped his tail once when he saw her. Paloma dropped to her knees beside him, soaking her jeans, and put her face against his warm neck. "I'm sorry," she whispered, over and over, into his fur. "I'm so sorry, I'm sorry." Then she scooped her arms under him, staggering, and called for her neighbor.

It's been an hour and Pepper hasn't come back in, and my husband is out looking on the street while I stand on the back step with my arms wrapped around myself. This afternoon, Pepper had been barking at the fence, nonstop, and I'd been on a work call, and I'd lost my temper. I'd gone out and yelled at her, really yelled, and swatted her rear end with a rolled-up magazine. She'd yelped and run to the corner of the yard and stayed there, ears flat. I'd felt bad for maybe five seconds and gone back inside. Now it's dark, and she's gone, and she's never once run off in four years. The hole under the fence by the lilac bush looks fresh. I keep picturing her flattened ears, the way she wouldn't look at me. I kneel down by the hole and put my hand in the dirt like I'll find her there. My throat is tight, my eyes hot. My husband's voice comes faintly from the street, calling her name. I start calling too, softly at first, in the voice I use when she's been good.

Darnell went to the window for the fifth time in ten minutes, pulling back the curtain and peering into the dark yard. No sign of Juno. His roommate's dog, not his. Marcus had gone home for the week and left Darnell with a list taped to the fridge: feed her twice, walk her twice, and do not, under any circumstances, leave her out in the yard alone, because she can jump the fence. Darnell had let her out alone at six because he'd wanted to finish a game online. He'd told himself five minutes. It had been two hours. He grabbed his jacket and went outside, his heart thudding, calling her name into the cold. A neighbor's porch light flicked on. He walked the block twice, shaking her leash, his voice cracking. Marcus texted: "How's my girl? Send a pic!" with a heart emoji. Darnell stared at the screen until it dimmed. He could not imagine answering it. He kept walking, his face burning in the cold air, checking under parked cars, behind dumpsters, and every shadow made his breath catch.

I didn't want a dog. I made that very clear to Ansel when he brought Moose home from the shelter. I said it in front of Moose, actually, a big gangly mutt sitting on our kitchen floor wagging his tail, and I said it pretty much every day for a year. I never played with him. I pushed him off the couch. I complained about the hair. Tonight Ansel is at his mother's and Moose went out at eight and hasn't come back, and I've been walking the yard with a flashlight for forty minutes, and I'm more frightened than I've ever been. I keep remembering last week, when Moose brought me his ball and dropped it at my feet and looked up at me, and I just stepped over it and went into the other room. He sat there by the ball for a long time. I saw him through the doorway. Now I'm on my knees, calling under the deck, my voice shaking, promising things to the dark: walks, treats, the whole couch. When I hear the jingle of his collar behind the shed, I nearly sob out loud.

Hyun-woo stood in the doorway in his socks, staring into the empty yard where his daughter's dog should have been. Mochi always came in when called. Always. He shook the food bowl. Nothing. Earlier that day, his daughter, Ji-eun, had asked if they could get the broken latch on the gate fixed. She'd asked last week too. And the week before. Each time he'd said, "This weekend," and each weekend he'd been tired, or there was a game on, or he simply hadn't felt like dealing with it. He walked out across the grass. The gate was swinging gently on its hinges, the latch hanging uselessly. His stomach dropped. Ji-eun was ten, and she was asleep upstairs, and the first thing she did every morning was run downstairs to feed Mochi. Hyun-woo grabbed a flashlight and went out into the street, calling the dog's name in a strained whisper so as not to wake the neighbors. He walked fast, then faster. His hands were damp. He kept seeing his daughter's face, asking about the latch, and how he'd barely looked up from his phone.

Backstage, I can hear the audience settling, that low rumble of chairs and coughing, and I keep looking at the setlist taped to the floor. The third song is called "Paper Boats," and everybody loves it; it's the one that got me signed. Rhys wrote the melody. My old bandmate. We were sitting on his bed in college and he was humming it, and I said, "That's nice," and two years later I recorded it under my own name with different lyrics. He never said anything. I heard through a friend that he'd stopped playing music altogether. The stage manager taps my shoulder: two minutes. My palms are wet. I wipe them on my jeans and they're wet again. I keep imagining Rhys somewhere in the audience, in the dark, though I know he isn't. I think about the royalty statements, the interviews where I've told the story of writing it alone at three in the morning. The lights go down. The crowd starts to cheer. I walk out into the glare, and when I get to the third song, my fingers fumble the first chord, and I have to start again.

Ayesha stood in the wings of the concert hall with her violin, waiting for her cue, and across the stage, she could see the empty chair where Benjamin should have been. He was the first chair violinist. He'd been asked to step down last month after his practice recordings had been anonymously sent to the conductor, recordings in which he'd played badly, sick with flu. Ayesha had sent them. She'd recorded him in the practice room without his knowledge and emailed the files from an account she'd made for the purpose. Now she was first chair. Tonight was her solo. She tightened her bow, and her fingers, which were usually so steady, couldn't seem to hold the screw. In the audience, somewhere in row G, Benjamin sat with his wife; he'd emailed her this morning to say break a leg. "You deserve it," he'd written. "Truly." The house lights dimmed. The conductor nodded at her. Ayesha walked out, raised the violin to her chin, and for one awful second, she could not remember the first note, could only see row G, the dark outline of his head.

Five minutes before I go on, my dad texts me a photo of himself in the hospital bed with the earbuds in, ready to listen to the livestream. He's in for his heart. I told him I couldn't come visit this week because of rehearsals. That wasn't really true. I could have driven up on Wednesday, three hours each way; I just didn't want to see him like that, with all the wires, his skin gray. I went to a movie instead. Now he's grinning in the photo, thumbs up, an IV taped to the back of his hand. He wrote, "Front row seat!!" with a pile of exclamation marks. I'm in the green room holding my guitar and I can't seem to tune it. The pegs keep slipping under my fingers. My bass player says, "You good?" and I nod. I'm not. I'm thinking about how I'm going to dedicate the last song to him, and how it'll sound noble, and how that'll be a lie too. They call my name. My legs carry me out there, and I sit down on the stool and look into the camera instead of the crowd.

Matteo adjusted the bench at the grand piano three times, though it was already at the right height. The hall was full, and somewhere in the third row sat Mrs. Ferraro, his first piano teacher, eighty years old now, invited by the festival as a surprise for him. They had put her photo in the program with a little tribute. What the program did not say was that he'd stopped taking lessons with her at fourteen, after his parents found a famous teacher in Milan, and that he'd told a newspaper, years later, that his early training had been "provincial, frankly limiting." She must have read it. Everyone in their town had read it. And still she'd come. During the applause before he began, he found her face in the audience, small and lined, beaming at him with her hands clasped. A heat rose up his neck. He placed his hands on the keys and they were trembling, which they never did. He played the first piece she had ever taught him, which was not on the program, and he could hear the audience shuffling their programs, confused, as he did.

It's a small venue, a café with folding chairs, maybe forty people, and I'm sitting on a stool at the back waiting for my turn, and the person going on before me is Lindiwe. Last month we both applied for the same grant, the one that would've paid for an album, and I won it. What nobody knows is that I was on the selection committee's email list by accident, and I saw the other applicants' recordings, and I re-recorded my demo to sound more like hers. I copied her arrangement. Hers was better. Now she's up there with an acoustic guitar, playing the song I stole the shape of, and it's even more beautiful live, and people are swaying, a woman in front is mouthing the words. Lindiwe looks happy. She told me before the show, "Congrats on the grant, by the way, you deserve it," and squeezed my arm. I keep turning my capo over in my hand. My mouth is dry. The applause swells when she finishes, and the host calls my name, and I don't stand up right away.

Felix had been asked to play at his brother's memorial, and he sat in the front pew with the cello case at his feet, waiting for the priest to finish. Everyone kept touching his shoulder. "He'd be so proud," they said. Felix nodded at each of them. He and Patrick had not spoken for the last two years of Patrick's life. It had been about money, about their father's house, about something Felix said at the reading of the will that couldn't be unsaid. Patrick had tried to call in March, then in April. Felix had watched his phone ring both times, and turned it face down on the table. In May, Patrick had died in his sleep. Now the priest was nodding toward him. Felix stood, opened the case, and lifted the cello out, and his hands were so cold he could barely feel the strings. He sat on the chair before the altar. He looked down at his brother's photograph, smiling, propped on an easel beside the flowers. He drew the bow across the first note, and it wavered, and he had to stop, and press his lips together, and begin again.

The box on my doorstep had my name on it in my aunt Philippa's looping handwriting, and I stood in the hallway turning it over before I could make myself open it. Inside, wrapped in tissue paper, was a quilt. A note was pinned to it: "I finished it at last! For your new baby. Sorry it took so long, my hands aren't what they were." My aunt has arthritis so bad she can barely hold a fork. She must have been working on it for a year. And I hadn't invited her to the baby shower. I'd told myself it was because she lives so far away, but really it was because she's loud and old-fashioned and I'd been worried she'd say something embarrassing in front of my husband's family. She'd found out anyway; my mother had mentioned it. I unfolded the quilt across the couch. Every square was a different fabric, and I recognized some of them: my grandfather's shirts, my childhood curtains. My fingers traced the uneven stitches, and my chest went tight and heavy. I sat down next to it, and I didn't move for a long time.

Callista didn't recognize the sender's name on the package, and when she opened it, she found a stack of her own textbooks, the ones she'd sold online last year, and a note. "Hi! I bought these from you for my nursing course," the note said. "I just graduated! I wanted to send them back because you'd written such nice notes in the margins, they really helped me through. Thank you." Callista sat down on the stairs. She remembered the transaction. The buyer, a girl named Esperanza, had messaged to ask if all the access codes were unused, because she couldn't afford to buy new ones. Callista had said yes. They'd all been used. She'd known that. She had pocketed the extra forty dollars for the codes and blocked the girl's account when she complained. Now Callista flipped open the anatomy book and saw her own handwriting, and next to it, in a different hand, small hearts and stars. Her cheeks burned. She looked for a return address on the box, found it, and wrote it on the back of her hand in pen, pressing so hard it hurt.

A package came addressed to the previous tenant, and I should have written "Not at this address" on it and put it back in the mailbox. That was two months ago. It's been sitting in my closet ever since, because when I shook it, it rattled like something expensive, and I thought, nobody will know. I opened it last week. A pair of noise-canceling headphones, top of the line. I've been wearing them on the train. This afternoon a second package came for the same name, a small padded envelope, and inside, because I opened that too, was a handwritten card. "Mateusz, I hope the headphones arrived okay. Your grandpa and I wanted you to be able to study in peace. We're so proud of you. Love, Babcia." I'm sitting on my bed with the card in my hand and the headphones around my neck, and they suddenly feel heavy as iron. There's a smiley face drawn next to the word Babcia. I take the headphones off and put them in my lap. I look at the old box in the closet and the tape I tore, and my stomach turns.

The package was from his son, Gareth, and Alistair stood in the kitchen holding it at arm's length, as if it might be dangerous. They hadn't spoken properly in six years, not since Alistair had refused to go to Gareth's wedding because Gareth was marrying a man. He'd said some things that day he could still hear in the quiet of the house. He opened the box slowly. Inside was a framed photograph of two men holding a baby, a little girl in a yellow knitted hat. On the back, in Gareth's careful handwriting: "Her name is Margaret, after Mum. We thought you should know. We'd like you to meet her, if you want." Alistair sat down at the kitchen table, his legs suddenly unsteady. His late wife's name. His granddaughter. He thought of what he'd said at the door, the slam of it, how Gareth had stood on the step and not cried until he'd turned away. Alistair put the photograph flat on the table and covered his eyes with one hand. The kettle began to whistle on the stove. He didn't get up to turn it off.

The box was wrapped in brown paper and tied with string, and the return address said it was from my old piano student, Lenka, who would be in her thirties now. Inside was a CD of her first album and a letter thanking me for being the teacher who believed in her. That's not what I remember. I remember a ten-year-old who couldn't keep time, and I remember telling her mother, within Lenka's hearing, that she had no real talent and they were wasting their money. I remember her face. She cried in the hallway while putting on her coat. Her mother pulled her out of lessons the next week. I'd been proud of my honesty then. Now I read her letter, in which she says that she practiced for years afterward to prove me wrong, and that she owes her career to that moment, and she sounds like she's trying to be gracious. I put the CD in the old player. The first track starts, and it's beautiful, and her timing is perfect. I sit on the sofa with my hands clenched, and my eyes start to sting.

When the courier handed Rahim the package, he signed for it absently, then saw the label: it was from the company where he'd worked until March. Inside was a farewell gift, a pen engraved with his name, and a card signed by the whole team. "We miss you!!" someone had written. "The office isn't the same." Another: "Thanks for always having our backs." Rahim's hands slowed as he read each one. He had left because he'd been offered a better job, yes, but before he went, he'd also handed his new employer a copy of the client list. Half his old team's accounts had moved over in the months since. He'd heard there had been layoffs. He read the signatures again, looking for the names of the people who'd been let go. There was Tanvir, who'd brought his famous samosas to every birthday. There was Joy, who'd covered his shift when his son was in the hospital. Both gone now, he thought. He put the pen back in its velvet case, closed it, and sat in his car in the driveway, staring at nothing, the card in his lap.

My sister Ines held up the jade bracelet and said, "Where's the matching ring? Grandma always said they were a set." I kept folding the scarves on the bed with my back to her. The ring was in my jewelry box at home. Grandma gave it to me last spring, when I visited for the first time in a year, and she'd said quietly, "Don't tell your sister, she'll fuss." I'd been so pleased. But I hadn't told Ines anything afterwards, and then Grandma died in August, and Ines had been the one at her bedside for the last three weeks, sleeping in the recliner, holding the cup while she drank. I was in Barcelona on a work trip. "Maybe she sold it," I said, and my voice came out thin. Ines frowned and kept searching the drawer, lifting old handkerchiefs and safety pins, and every time she lifted something my stomach twisted harder. She found an old photograph of Grandma wearing both pieces, and she smiled at it, sadly, and showed it to me. I couldn't take it from her hand. I said I needed some air and went out onto the porch, my face hot.

The three of them worked in silence in their grandmother's bedroom, sorting clothes into bags for charity. Aurelio was the eldest, and he kept stopping to look at the papers in her desk, because he was the one who had handled her finances for the last five years. His sisters didn't know about the money he'd borrowed. Ten thousand dollars, from her savings, for his failing restaurant; he'd told himself he'd pay it back before anyone noticed. She had noticed. She'd said nothing, only patted his hand and told him to take care of himself. Now Valentina was opening the bank folder, frowning at a statement. "This doesn't look right," she said. "Was there a big withdrawal in 2021?" Aurelio's chest tightened. "Medical stuff, I think," he said, and immediately felt the lie burn in his throat. His younger sister, Pilar, was holding up their grandmother's favorite cardigan and crying softly into it. Aurelio looked from one sister to the other, his hands gripping the back of the desk chair, and opened his mouth, and closed it, and finally sat down heavily on the bed.

Sorting Nana's things, my brother Hamish found the stack of birthday cards I'd sent her. There were only four of them. She'd kept every single one, rubber-banded together with a note in her shaky handwriting: "From Ewan." Four cards in twenty years. Hamish's stack, by comparison, filled an entire shoebox. He didn't say anything, which was worse; he just handed them to me and went back to the bookshelf. I opened the top one. It was a generic card from a gas station, with a scrawled "Happy B-day Nana, love E." She'd underlined the word love. My throat got tight. I'd lived thirty minutes away. I could have visited every Sunday. Hamish had moved to the other side of the country and still called her every week. Downstairs our mother was talking to the estate agent, her voice echoing through the empty rooms. I sat on Nana's floral bedspread holding those four cards and couldn't stop staring at the underlined word. When Hamish asked if I was okay, I nodded and said it was just dust, and rubbed my eyes with the back of my wrist.

Soo-ah and her younger brother had promised each other they would not fight over anything, and so far they hadn't, though there wasn't much worth fighting over: a few dresses, some cooking pots, a box of photographs. What Soo-ah kept looking at was the old armchair by the window. Their grandmother had spent the last two years of her life in that chair, mostly alone. Soo-ah had moved her into the small apartment after their grandfather died, promising to visit every weekend, and then had visited every month, then every few months. Her brother, who lived abroad, had never known. Now he sat down in the chair and found, tucked in the side cushion, a calendar. On every Saturday, their grandmother had drawn a small circle. A few of them, very few, had check marks. The rest were just empty circles, week after week. "What do you think these were?" he asked, puzzled, flipping the pages. Soo-ah felt her face drain. She knew exactly. She reached for the calendar, then pulled her hand back, and turned to the window so he wouldn't see her eyes filling.

My brother Desmond says Gran's dog should go to the shelter because neither of us has room. I agree too quickly. Rusty is a fat old terrier, gray-muzzled, and he's lying in the hallway with his head on Gran's slippers, watching us carry boxes past. She asked me, in the hospital, to take him if anything happened. She squeezed my fingers and said, "He'll only eat if you sit with him." I told her of course, I promised. I didn't tell Desmond about that. My apartment doesn't allow pets, technically, but I know people who have cats there. I could make it work. I just don't want to. Desmond's on the phone with the shelter now, asking about their hours, and Rusty lifts his head when I walk past and thumps his tail on the floor, once, twice. I stop. My heart hammers. I crouch down and he licks my wrist. I remember her hand on mine, her voice going faint. "Hang up," I say to Desmond, too loud, and he stares at me. "Just hang up. I'm taking him."

Olamide and her sister Folake sat on the floor of their grandmother's sitting room with the jewelry box between them. Folake was the one who'd suggested splitting everything evenly, and she'd been generous all afternoon, letting Olamide choose first each time. Olamide couldn't look at her for long. Last year, when their grandmother was writing her will, she had asked Olamide to help, and Olamide had steered her, subtly, gently, toward leaving the house to Olamide alone. "Folake has her husband's money," she'd said. "She doesn't need it." Their grandmother had been confused and tired and had agreed. The will would be read next week. Folake had no idea. Now Folake held up a pair of coral earrings and said, "You should have these, Grandma always said they matched your eyes." She pressed them into Olamide's palm and folded her fingers over them. Olamide felt something hard catch in her throat. The earrings were cold and smooth, and she clutched them so tightly the clasps pricked her skin. She could not say thank you. She looked down at the carpet, at its faded pattern of vines, and kept looking.

Monday morning, I roll up the metal shutter on the bakery and the first thing I see is the little hand-lettered sign taped to the inside of the door: "Sorry, closed Saturday due to illness." I wasn't sick. I went to my cousin's beach house for the weekend on a whim and didn't want to tell anyone. The sign is in Mrs. Adeyemi's handwriting. She's my assistant baker, sixty-three, and she came in at four on Saturday morning like she always does, found it empty, and when she couldn't reach me, she worried I was in the hospital. I know this because she left me four voicemails, each one more frightened, and I didn't listen to them until Sunday night on the drive home, sunburnt and happy. Now she comes through the back door and her face floods with relief. "You're all right!" she says, and hugs me, flour on her hands. I hug her back stiffly. She asks what it was, a fever? I say a stomach thing and look away, busying myself with the ovens, and my ears burn as she tells me to take it easy today, and that she'll do the heavy trays.

Rizwan unlocked the hardware store at seven, as he had every Monday for twenty-two years, and stood for a moment in the dim aisle with the keys still in his hand. On Friday a man had come in looking for a replacement part for a space heater. Rizwan had been busy and tired and had sold him the wrong one, a cheaper part from the bin, and when the man asked if it would fit, Rizwan had said, "Should do." He'd known it might not. Over the weekend he'd heard about the fire on Delancey Street. A small one. Nobody hurt, the paper said, but a family's living room gutted, caused by a faulty heater. He did not know if it was the same man. He had no way to know. He switched on the lights and the fluorescents flickered and buzzed overhead. He walked to the heating aisle and stood looking at the bin of parts, picking them up and putting them down, reading the numbers stamped on them. When the bell over the door jangled with the first customer, he flinched so hard he dropped one on the floor.

I open the flower shop at eight on Mondays and the first job is always the same: check what's still fresh, toss what isn't. This morning I open the cooler and the bucket of white lilies is there, the ones I was supposed to deliver on Saturday to the Ostrowski funeral. I forgot. I was busy with a wedding order, a big one that paid well, and I put the funeral on the back burner and then it just slipped away. The lilies are drooping, browning at the edges. The family had chosen them specially; the daughter had told me on the phone that her mother had grown them in her garden for forty years. I check my voicemail. Two messages from Saturday afternoon, a woman's voice, polite and then confused and then very quiet. "We had to go ahead without them," the second one says. "I just wanted to make sure you're okay." I lean against the cold steel shelf. My face is hot even in the chill of the cooler. I pick up a lily and its petals fall in my hand. I stand there a long time before I go to find her number.

Wilhelmina unlocked the café door at six-thirty and saw the envelope that had been slid underneath it. She knew what it would say before she picked it up. Last Wednesday, she'd fired her youngest barista, Kieran, for stealing from the till. The drawer had been short three hundred dollars, and he'd been the last one closing. He'd sworn he hadn't taken it. Then, on Saturday, she'd found the money, in the deposit bag, in her own car, under the passenger seat, where she'd tossed it in a rush on her way to the bank. She'd sat in the car with the bag in her lap for twenty minutes. She hadn't called him. She'd meant to; she'd picked up her phone half a dozen times. The envelope had his name on the front. Inside was his uniform apron, folded neatly, and a note: "I still didn't do it. But thank you for the job." Wilhelmina sank down onto one of the chairs that were still upside down on the table, nearly knocking it over, and held the apron against her chest. The coffee machine hissed as it warmed up behind her.

Monday, 9 a.m., and the bookstore is quiet except for the radiator ticking, and I'm standing behind the counter staring at the stack of flyers for Zainab's reading this Thursday. Zainab is a local poet, first book, and she asked me months ago if she could launch it here. I said yes. Then last Friday, a big-name author's publicist called and offered me a signing for the same night, guaranteed hundreds of sales, and I said yes to that too. I haven't told Zainab. I've been composing the email all weekend. Every draft starts with "Unfortunately" and I delete it. Her flyers are lovely. She designed them herself, with a little drawing of the shop's front window, my window, with the cat asleep in it. She dropped them off herself on Saturday, and brought a tin of homemade shortbread for me. It's still sitting on the counter, half eaten. I pick up a flyer and look at the little cat. My stomach is sour. I flip the shop sign to OPEN and sit down at my laptop and stare at the empty email, my hands not moving.

Hideo pulled up the shutter of the noodle shop and the morning light fell across the counter where, on Saturday, he had snapped at the delivery boy. The boy, a teenager from the neighborhood named Shun, had been ten minutes late, and Hideo, short-staffed and furious, had shouted at him in front of customers, had called him lazy and useless, had told him not to bother coming back. Shun had gone pale and left without a word. On Sunday, Hideo's wife had told him: the boy's mother had been in the hospital since Friday night. He had been late because he'd stayed with her. Now Hideo stood in his empty shop with the cold broth pots, the stacked bowls, the quiet. His wife hadn't said anything more, but she had looked at him in a way that had kept him awake. He set out the chairs one by one, more slowly than usual. Then he took a container from the shelf and filled it with yesterday's best broth, the one with the extra pork bone, and wrapped it in a cloth, and stood holding it by the door, his throat tight, trying to gather himself to go.

The line at the food bank stretches out the door into the cold, and I'm handing out cans of soup and boxes of pasta, smiling, saying, "Have a good day." I signed up for this because I needed community service hours for a job application, and I've been counting the minutes since I got here. Then a woman reaches the front of the line and I recognize her. It's Mrs. Tran, who used to run the dry cleaner's on Fifth, where my father took his suits. Last year I wrote a scathing online review of her shop because they'd lost a button on my blazer. One star. I called her careless. I told everyone in our neighborhood group chat to avoid the place. The shop closed in the spring. Now she's standing in front of me holding a reusable bag, and she doesn't recognize me, and she thanks me with a little bow of her head. My hands freeze around the can of beans. I put an extra jar of peanut butter in her bag, then another, my cheeks blazing, and I can't make myself meet her tired, grateful eyes.

Ruth had been volunteering at the food bank every Tuesday for six years, and everyone said she was a saint. She organized the canned goods by expiration date. She remembered the children's names. Today, though, she couldn't stop glancing at the back storeroom, at the cardboard box of donated gift cards she had taken home last December. Grocery cards, fifty dollars each, a dozen of them, meant for families during the holidays. Her husband had lost his job that autumn, and they had been behind on the mortgage, and she'd told herself it was just this once, that she was a family in need too. Nobody had noticed. Now the coordinator, a cheerful young man named Jasper, was explaining that this year they'd be giving out gift cards again, and wouldn't it be wonderful, and could Ruth take charge of it, since she was the most trustworthy person he knew. Ruth smiled and said yes. Her hands were shaking as she stacked the cans. When a little girl in line held up her drawing of a turkey to show her, Ruth bent down to admire it and could hardly speak.

I'm volunteering at the food bank because my therapist suggested it, and I'm sorting donated produce into crates when I see the bag of apples someone has dropped off from my own neighbor's tree. I know because there's a note on it in Mr. Delacroix's handwriting, "Picked this morning! Enjoy!" Last month his tree dropped apples over the fence into my yard, and I complained to the city, and he got a fine, and the city told him he had to cut back the branches. He did it. He cut half the tree down. He's eighty-something, and I watched him do it from my window, sawing slowly, resting on the stepladder every few minutes. I never went out to help. I never said a word. Now I'm holding his apples, red and lopsided and perfect, and the other volunteers are exclaiming over how fresh they look. One of them takes a bite and says it's the best apple she's had in years. I put the bag down gently in the crate. My chest aches. I keep thinking of the sound of that saw, back and forth, back and forth, all afternoon.

Duncan had come to the food bank with his church group, and he was assigned to the intake desk, writing down names and household sizes. He did not expect to see his younger brother walk in. Fraser stopped dead when he saw him. They hadn't spoken since their mother's funeral two years ago, when Duncan had told him, in front of the whole family, that he was a disgrace and a drunk and he'd killed their mother with worry. Fraser looked thinner now, older, clean-shaven, a sober chip on a cord around his neck. He came forward slowly, holding a crumpled form. Duncan's hands went cold on the pen. He wrote his brother's name on the sheet. Household size: one. Fraser's eyes stayed on the table. "Hey, Dunc," he said quietly. Duncan's face burned. He stood up, didn't know what to do with his hands, sat back down. Behind Fraser, the line shuffled forward. Duncan wanted to say something, anything, but his throat had closed entirely, and he just handed him the ticket for his box and watched him walk away, his own pen trembling in his hand.

I'm on the produce table at the food bank, and every time someone passes, I hand them a bag of carrots or potatoes and wish them a good weekend. This is my first shift. I came because, two weeks ago, I threw out an entire refrigerator of food. I'd been away, and I came back and everything had gone soft, and I just swept it all into black bags without thinking, three of them, enough to fill a car trunk. My building's janitor, Augustin, saw me carrying the bags out and asked, very gently, if there was anything in there still good, because his sister had five kids and her husband had just lost his job. I said no, all spoiled, and dropped them in the dumpster. Some of it wasn't spoiled. The cheese, the eggs, the frozen chicken. I knew it as I was saying it. And now a woman comes through the line with five children, five, the littlest on her hip, and she's got Augustin's same wide cheekbones. My hand stops in mid-air with the carrots. She smiles and takes them. I fill her bags with everything I'm allowed, then a bit more, my eyes blurring.

Priyanka had volunteered at the food bank for her college application, and she'd posted a photo of herself in the blue apron with the caption "Giving back is everything." It had gotten three hundred likes. She'd been there for forty-five minutes total that day. She'd left early, claiming a headache, and asked the coordinator to sign off on six hours, which he had, without checking. Now she was back, months later, because the admissions office had called to verify, and she'd panicked and said she was still volunteering. The coordinator, a gray-haired woman named Mrs. Okonkwo, greeted her with a hug. "Our celebrity!" she said. "That photo of yours brought us twelve new volunteers!" Priyanka laughed weakly. She was given a station unpacking a truck of donated cans and worked through the whole morning without stopping, her arms aching, her back damp with sweat. Every time Mrs. Okonkwo passed and patted her shoulder, Priyanka bent lower over the boxes. At noon, when the others broke for lunch, she kept working, stacking can after can, unable to stop.

The waiting room smells of disinfectant and burnt coffee, and I've been staring at the same page of a magazine for an hour. My husband is in surgery. They said four hours, maybe five. He fell off the ladder cleaning the gutters, the job he'd been asking me to help with for weeks. "Just hold the ladder," he'd said, every Saturday. And every Saturday I'd said I was busy, or I'd do it next weekend, or why couldn't he hire someone. Yesterday he'd gone up alone. I was inside on the couch with my phone when I heard him shout and the clatter. My hands are still shaking, even now. Every time the doors swing open, I half rise out of my chair. A nurse comes out and calls another family's name, and I sink back down, my heart pounding. A woman across from me offers me a granola bar and I can't take it. I keep thinking of him at breakfast, asking one more time, so politely, the way he always does, and me rolling my eyes and saying, "Not now, I've had a long week."

Ezekiel sat in the plastic chair, elbows on his knees, staring at the linoleum. His daughter had been brought in by ambulance three hours ago. Alcohol poisoning at a college party, they'd said. She was nineteen. A nurse had told him she was stable now, and that he could see her soon, and he'd nodded and said thank you, but his mind was somewhere else: on the weekend she'd turned sixteen, when he'd given her a beer at the barbecue and laughed when she made a face, and on all the times after that, the glasses of wine with dinner, the jokes about how she could hold her drink like her old man. He'd thought it was harmless. He'd thought he was being a cool dad. Her mother had warned him, and he'd called her uptight. Now a man in scrubs was walking toward him with a clipboard, and Ezekiel stood up so fast his knees buckled. "You can see her now," the doctor said. Ezekiel followed him down the hall, his feet heavy, his breath short, afraid of what he'd see on her face when she looked at him.

I'm in the hospital waiting room because my best friend tried to hurt herself last night, and I am the person she texted first. I didn't answer. I saw the message at eleven, "can you call me," and I was tired and I'd had a long day of hearing about her bad week, and I thought, I'll call her in the morning. Her roommate found her at two. Now her parents are sitting across from me holding hands, and her mother keeps thanking me for coming, for being such a good friend to her. I nod and stare at the vending machine, at the rows of chips and candy, counting them, because if I look at her mother I'll fall apart. My phone is in my lap, face down. I keep turning it over to look at that message, then turning it back. Can you call me. Four words. The fluorescent light above me flickers. Her father gets up to get coffee and asks if I want some. I shake my head. My jaw is clenched so hard it aches, and I keep thinking about how easy it would have been.

Leonora sat in the corner of the waiting room with her coat still on, though it was warm, and watched the doors to the intensive care unit. Her mother was in there. The doctors said she'd had a fall at home, alone, and had lain on the kitchen floor for two days before a neighbor noticed. Two days. Leonora usually called her every Sunday. Last Sunday she hadn't. She'd been at a friend's wedding, and then hungover, and then it was Monday and she was busy, and she'd thought, oh, Mum will be fine, I'll call midweek. She had not called midweek. She kept doing the arithmetic over and over: the fall had happened Sunday evening. If she'd called, her mother wouldn't have answered. She would have known something was wrong. Leonora twisted the strap of her handbag around her fingers until they went white. A doctor came out and called, "Family of Mrs. Bassett?" and Leonora stood up, and her knees were so weak she had to put a hand on the chair. She followed him through the doors, her face hot, rehearsing an apology she did not know how to begin.

It's my grandfather in there, having a procedure on his heart, and I'm here because my mom asked me to sit with him while she drove in from work. I said I would. I was supposed to be here at nine. I got here at eleven. I'd overslept, then gotten coffee, then sat in my car scrolling through my phone because I didn't really want to come. When I finally walked in, the receptionist told me they'd already taken him back and that he'd asked for me twice. "He was a little anxious," she said kindly. "Kept looking at the door." Now I'm sitting in a vinyl chair across from the TV, which is playing a cooking show nobody is watching, and I can't stop picturing him on that gurney in his thin gown, his hands knotted together, craning his neck. He's eighty-seven. He drove me to school every single day for six years when my parents were working. Not once was he late. I'm picking at my thumbnail until it bleeds, and I wipe it on my jeans, and I watch the doors, waiting to be allowed through so I can tell him I'm here.

Sunil sat in the waiting room of the children's ward, holding his son's backpack in his lap, the one with the dinosaur keychain. Arun had broken his arm falling off the climbing frame at the park. Sunil had been on a bench thirty feet away answering work emails when it happened. He'd told Arun to go play and not bother him for ten minutes, and he'd said it sharply, because the boy had been tugging at his sleeve, wanting him to watch him climb to the top. "Watch me, Papa, watch!" Sunil had said, "Not now." He'd heard the scream and dropped his phone. The doctors said it was a clean break, that kids heal quickly. Through the little window in the door, he could see Arun on the bed, a nurse wrapping his arm in blue plaster, and the boy was being brave, biting his lip, glancing toward the door for his father. Sunil kept turning the dinosaur keychain around in his fingers. His eyes were burning. He thought of the email he'd been answering, which was about nothing, nothing at all, and he pressed his knuckles hard against his mouth.
